Section 1

Why this one paper matters so much

In 2017, a team at Google published a short paper — only eight pages long — with a bold title. It described a new kind of neural network called the Transformer. (A neural network is just a computer program that learns from examples. We will explain it properly very soon.) The paper made a surprising claim. You could throw away the two main ideas people had used for years to handle language, and replace them with one simpler idea called attention.

That bet worked far better than anyone expected. The Transformer is now the design inside GPT, Claude, Gemini, LLaMA, BERT, and almost every system people call "AI" today. If you want to understand modern AI — or work at a company that builds it — this is the paper to start with. Reading it carefully is one of the most useful things you can do.

Key idea · the whole paper in one sentence

A Transformer looks at every word in a sentence at the same time. It lets each word decide which other words to "pay attention to" when working out its own meaning. That one simple idea turned out to be enough to beat older models that read words one at a time.

The rest of these notes will explain that sentence fully. We will start at the very beginning — even from what "turning a word into numbers" means.

Section 2

The problem it was built to solve

The paper's main example is translation: read a sentence in English, then write the same sentence in German. This is one example of a bigger task the authors call sequence transduction. That is a fancy phrase for a simple thing: turning one ordered list into another ordered list.

From zero · what is a "sequence"?

A sequence is just a list where the order matters. A sentence is a sequence of words. "The cat sat" is three words in a set order. Order changes meaning: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" use the same words but mean opposite things. So any program that handles language must respect order. Keep this in mind — it comes back in Section 8.

Translation is hard because words that are far apart in a sentence often depend on each other. To translate one word correctly, you sometimes need a word from much earlier. Here is an example: "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired." What does "it" mean — the animal or the street? To get this right, you have to connect "it" back to "animal," which sits eight words earlier. A good model needs an easy way to link faraway words. Remember this idea. It is exactly what attention makes easy.

So how did people build these models before 2017? Almost all of them used a two-part shape called the encoder–decoder. And almost all of them read text one word at a time, using something called a recurrent network. To see why the Transformer was such a big step, we first need to understand that older way of doing things. That means learning a few real basics first.

Section 3

Foundations, built from zero

This section gives you the five basic ideas you need before the Transformer makes sense: turning words into numbers, what a "layer" does, softmax, the encoder–decoder shape, and finally recurrent networks and their big weakness. If you already know these, feel free to skim. If you don't, this is the part that makes everything else click.

3.1  Tokens and embeddings — turning words into numbers

A neural network can only do math. It cannot work with the letters "c-a-t" directly. So the first step in any language model is to turn text into numbers. This happens in two steps.

Step one: tokenisation. The text is cut into small pieces called tokens. A token is often a whole word. But for rare or long words, it can be a word-piece. For example, "tokenisation" might split into "token" + "isation." The paper cuts text into about 37,000 possible pieces. Why use pieces? Because a small, fixed set of pieces can build any word — even a word the model has never seen before.

Step two: embedding. Each token is then turned into a vector — a list of numbers — called its embedding. In this paper, every embedding is a list of 512 numbers. You can picture each token as a dot in space, where tokens with similar meanings sit close together. "King" sits near "queen." "Paris" sits near "France." The model learns these numbers on its own during training. Nobody sets them by hand.

From zero · what is a vector, really?

A vector is just a list of numbers. [2, 0] is a vector with two numbers. The word "cat" might become a list of 512 numbers like [0.21, −1.03, 0.88, …]. Why so many numbers? Because meaning is rich, and 512 numbers give the model enough room to capture small differences. Two simple actions on vectors will show up again and again. One is adding them (add the matching numbers). The other is the dot product: multiply the matching numbers, then add up the results. The dot product is large when two vectors point in a similar direction. So it works as a similarity score — a way to measure how alike two things are. Remember that; attention is built on it.

3.2  What a neural-network "layer" actually does

The word "layer" sounds mysterious, but the main action is simple. The basic move is called a linear layer (also called a "fully-connected" or "dense" layer). You take an input list of numbers, multiply it by a grid of learned numbers (called a weight matrix), and add another learned list (called a bias). In short: output $= xW + b$. In plain terms, this stretches, turns, and shifts the input numbers.

Stacking these linear layers alone is useless, because many linear steps in a row still add up to just one linear step. So between them we add a nonlinearity: a small function that bends the numbers. The paper uses one called ReLU. It is about as simple as a rule can be: change every negative number to zero, and leave positive numbers alone. In symbols: $\operatorname{ReLU}(x)=\max(0,x)$. Linear layers plus these bends, stacked together, can copy very complicated patterns. That is the whole engine of deep learning.

From zero · what does "learned" mean?

Every weight matrix starts out as random numbers. During training, the model makes a guess, we measure how wrong it was compared to the right answer, and then math nudges every number a tiny bit in the direction that would have made the guess better. Do this millions of times, and the random numbers slowly turn into a working model. You do not need the math to read this paper. Just hold on to one idea: the weights are like knobs, and training is the process of turning them.

3.3  Softmax — turning scores into a choice

Often we have a few raw scores, and we want to turn them into weights that are all positive and add up to 1. (Weights that add up to 1 are handy, because they act like shares of a whole.) The function that does this is softmax. It makes every score positive and stretches the gaps between them, then divides so the results add up to one.

$$\operatorname{softmax}(z)_i=\dfrac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j} e^{z_j}}$$

Here is an example. The scores [1, 2, 4] become about [0.04, 0.11, 0.85]. The biggest score takes most of the weight, but the smaller ones still keep a little. Softmax shows up in two places in the Transformer: inside attention (to decide how much weight to give each word) and at the very end (to turn the model's final numbers into the chances for the next word). Keep one fact in mind: when the gaps between scores are bigger, softmax gets sharper — closer to "winner takes all." That fact matters in Section 4.

3.4  The encoder–decoder shape

Most translation models, including the Transformer, split into two halves:

  • The encoder reads the whole input sentence and turns it into a set of rich number-summaries. Think of it as the part that understands the input.
  • The decoder takes those summaries and writes the output sentence one word at a time. Each time, it looks at both what the encoder understood and what it has written so far.

The decoder is auto-regressive. That word just means it uses the words it has already written to help write the next one. To write word 5, it feeds back words 1 to 4 that it already produced. This "write a word, feed it back, write the next" loop is exactly how ChatGPT writes a sentence, one word at a time.

3.5  Recurrent networks and the bottleneck that doomed them

Before the Transformer, the encoder and decoder were usually recurrent neural networks (RNNs). (The famous LSTM and GRU are types of RNN.) An RNN reads a sequence strictly in order. As it reads, it keeps a running memory called a hidden state. It reads word 1 and updates its memory. It reads word 2 and updates again. And so on. Each step needs the result of the step before it.

That "each step needs the one before" rule is the big problem. Two troubles come straight from it:

  1. No working in parallel. Because step 5 needs step 4, you cannot do the steps at the same time — even on a fast chip (a GPU) that has thousands of cores sitting idle. So training is slow, and it gets slower for longer sentences.
  2. Forgetting over long distances. Information from word 1 has to pass through every step, and survive being changed each time, before it reaches word 50. The signal gets weaker along this long path. So linking faraway words (our "it" → "animal" problem) is genuinely hard for an RNN.
Key idea · the motivation

The Transformer was built to fix both RNN problems at once. It makes the work fully parallel (fast on GPUs). And it makes the path between any two words just one step long (so faraway links are easy to learn). Attention is the trick that does both.

Section 4

The core idea: attention

Attention is the heart of the paper. Once you understand it, everything else is just wiring. We will build it in three steps: first the idea, then the exact formula, then a small example with real numbers. After that, we will explain the one odd-looking detail — dividing by a square root.

4.1  The idea: queries, keys, and values

Imagine each word wants to collect information from the other words to understand itself better. The word "it" is basically asking the sentence: "which earlier word am I standing for?" Attention is a precise way to ask questions like this and to mix the answers together.

The paper gives each word three roles. Each role is just a vector built from the word:

  • Query (Q) — what this word is looking for. ("I am a pronoun, and I am looking for my noun.")
  • Key (K) — the label each word offers, so it can be matched against queries. ("I am a single animal noun.")
  • Value (V) — the actual information a word will hand over if it gets attended to. ("Here is my meaning.")
Intuition · the library search

Think of searching for a book. What you type is the query. Every book has a key (its title or subject on the spine) and a value (what is actually inside). You compare what you typed against every key to see how well each one matches. Then you read the contents of the books that match — paying more attention to the better matches. Attention does exactly this. The one difference: it does not pick a single book. It takes a weighted blend of all the values, giving more weight to the keys that matched your query best.

Where do Q, K, and V come from? Each word's embedding is multiplied by three different learned weight matrices (remember §3.2): $W^Q$, $W^K$, and $W^V$. These produce that word's query, key, and value. The model learns what makes a good query, key, and value during training.

4.2  Scaled Dot-Product Attention, step by step

Here is the method the authors call Scaled Dot-Product Attention. Read the four steps first. After that, the formula will look obvious.

  1. Score. For one query, take its dot product with every key. (Remember: dot product = similarity. A high score means "this key matters to my query.")
  2. Scale. Divide every score by $\sqrt{d_k}$. Here $d_k$ is the length of the key vectors. (We explain why in §4.4. For now, just know it keeps the numbers from getting too big.)
  3. Softmax. Push the scaled scores through softmax (§3.3) so they become positive weights that add up to 1. These are the attention weights: how much this query pays attention to each word.
  4. Blend. Multiply each word's value by its weight, then add them all up. The result is the answer for this query: a custom mix of the whole sentence, leaning toward whatever mattered most.

In real use, we don't handle one query at a time. We stack all the queries into a grid called $Q$, all the keys into $K$, and all the values into $V$. Then we do every dot product at once with a single matrix multiplication. Doing it all at once is the whole point (§3.5). The full method is this one line — equation (1) of the paper:

$$\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$ paper eq. (1)

Let's match it to the four steps. $QK^{\top}$ is score. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ is scale. $\operatorname{softmax}(\cdot)$ makes the weights. Multiplying by $V$ is the blend. That is the whole method. Nothing happens in order, one step after another — every answer is worked out together.

4.3  A tiny worked example

Worked example · 3 keys, 1 query

Suppose the word "it" makes a query. After the score-and-scale step, its scores against three earlier words come out like this: animal → 4.0, street → 1.0, was → 0.5. Softmax turns these into weights of about animal 0.93, street 0.05, was 0.02. So the answer handed to "it" is about 93% the value of "animal," with a little of the others mixed in. In effect, the model has worked out what "it" refers to: "it" now mostly carries the meaning of "animal." This really happens — see Figure 3 in Section 11, where attention links a pronoun to its noun.

4.4  Why divide by √dk? (the one tricky bit)

This scaling step is the only part of the formula that is not obvious. The paper explains it in a footnote that is worth unpacking. When you take the dot product of two random vectors of length $d_k$, the result tends to get bigger as $d_k$ gets bigger. (To be exact, its spread — called variance — equals $d_k$.) So with the 64-number keys used here, raw scores can swing into the tens or hundreds.

Why is that bad? Remember that softmax gets sharper as the gaps grow (§3.3). If you feed it very big scores, it puts almost all the weight on one word — basically "winner takes all." When softmax gets that extreme, a problem appears: its gradients become tiny. (A gradient is the small nudge that training uses to improve the model.) Tiny gradients mean the model can barely learn, so training gets stuck. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ shrinks the scores back to a calm range (spread close to 1). That keeps softmax responsive and easy to train.

Section 5

Multi-head attention

Doing attention once gives each word one blended summary. But a word connects to its surroundings in many ways at the same time. There is grammar (what is my subject?), meaning (what is the topic?), and position (what is nearby?). Forcing all of that through a single attention step is limiting. The authors point out that one attention step tends to blur these different relationships together, because it averages them.

The fix is multi-head attention. You run several attention steps side by side, at the same time. Each one has its own learned $W^Q$, $W^K$, $W^V$. So each "head" can focus on a different kind of relationship. Each head works in a smaller space. Then you join their outputs together and pass them through one more learned matrix, $W^O$, to combine them.

$$\operatorname{MultiHead}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{Concat}(\text{head}_1,\dots,\text{head}_h)\,W^{O}$$ $$\text{where}\quad \text{head}_i=\operatorname{Attention}(QW_i^{Q},\,KW_i^{K},\,VW_i^{V})$$
Intuition · a small group of specialists

Instead of asking one expert to think about every angle, you ask a small group. One person watches grammar. Another watches meaning. Another watches who-refers-to-whom. Each studies the sentence on their own, and then you combine their notes. That is multi-head attention. In Section 11 you will see that real heads really do specialise like this.

A clever detail: the paper uses $h=8$ heads, and makes each head smaller, with size $d_k=d_v=d_{model}/h = 512/8 = 64$. Because each head is one-eighth the size, running eight of them costs about the same as running one full-size head. You get many points of view almost for free.

Section 6

The three places attention is used

The same multi-head attention is reused in three roles inside the model. The only thing that changes is where Q, K, and V come from. This is worth getting clear, because it often confuses people.

  1. Encoder self-attention. Q, K, and V all come from the encoder's previous layer. Every input word looks at every other input word to build context. "Self" means the sentence is looking at itself.
  2. Decoder self-attention (masked). Q, K, and V all come from the decoder's previous layer — but with a mask. The mask lets each output word look only at earlier output words, never at future ones (more in §7.4). This keeps the auto-regressive rule: you cannot peek at words you have not written yet.
  3. Encoder–decoder attention. The queries come from the decoder, while the keys and values come from the encoder's output. This is the bridge. It lets each word being written look back at the whole input sentence.
Key idea

One method, three wirings. Self-attention means Q, K, and V come from the same place (a sentence looking at itself). Cross-attention (encoder–decoder) means the queries come from one place and the keys and values from another (the decoder looking at the encoder).

Section 7

The full architecture, box by box

You now know every part. Here is the paper's full diagram, and we will walk through it piece by piece. The left tower is the encoder. The right tower is the decoder. Data flows upward. The "N×" labels mean the whole block is stacked 6 times.

7.1  The encoder stack

The encoder is a stack of 6 identical layers. Each layer has exactly two parts, in this order:

  1. a multi-head self-attention part (§5–6), which lets each word gather context from all the others;
  2. a position-wise feed-forward network (§7.3), which works on each word on its own.

Both parts are wrapped in the "Add & Norm" step described next. Every part, and the embeddings, output lists of $d_{model}=512$ numbers, so the pieces fit together neatly.

7.2  "Add & Norm": residual connections + layer normalisation

Those yellow "Add & Norm" boxes show up after every part. They bundle two standard tricks that make deep networks possible to train.

Add — the residual connection. Instead of replacing its input, each part adds its output to its input: output $=x+\operatorname{Sublayer}(x)$. So the part only has to learn a small change (a "residual"). This also builds a clear path for the training signal to travel straight back through many layers without fading away. It is the same idea that let image networks (called ResNets) get very deep.

Norm — layer normalisation. After adding, the result is normalised: re-centred and re-scaled so its numbers stay in a steady range. This stops the numbers from growing too big or shrinking too small as they pass through 6 or more layers. That makes training faster and more stable. Put together:

$$\operatorname{LayerNorm}\bigl(x+\operatorname{Sublayer}(x)\bigr)$$
From zero · why bother?

If you just stack many layers, the training signal tends to either blow up or fade to nothing by the time it reaches the early layers — and then the network can't learn. Residual connections (a clean add-back path) and normalisation (keeping numbers calm) are the two everyday fixes that make deep stacks like this one work. You will see "Add & Norm" in almost every Transformer ever built.

7.3  Position-wise feed-forward network

After attention has let a word gather context, the feed-forward network (FFN) gives the word room to think about what it gathered. It is two linear layers (§3.2) with a ReLU in between, applied to each word separately and in the same way:

$$\operatorname{FFN}(x)=\max(0,\,xW_1+b_1)\,W_2+b_2$$ paper eq. (2)

Look at the sizes. It grows from $d_{model}=512$ numbers up to an inner width of $d_{ff}=2048$, applies ReLU, then shrinks back down to 512. Growing and then shrinking gives the model extra room to reshape each word. "Position-wise" just means the same small network is used on every word on its own. No words mix here — that already happened in the attention part. (The authors note this is the same as two convolutions with a window size of 1.)

Intuition · gather, then think

An easy way to remember one Transformer layer: attention is where each word gathers useful information from the sentence. The feed-forward network is where each word thinks privately about what it gathered. Repeat these two moves six times, and understanding gets deeper.

7.4  The decoder stack and the causal mask

The decoder is also 6 identical layers. But each one has three parts instead of two:

  1. Masked multi-head self-attention (over the output written so far);
  2. Encoder–decoder attention (queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder — the bridge from §6);
  3. the same position-wise feed-forward network.

The new and important word is masked. The decoder writes left to right. So when it works out the word at position $i$, it must not look at positions $i{+}1, i{+}2, \dots$ — those are the future words it is supposed to predict. If it could see them, training would be cheating, and real writing would be impossible.

The way they do this is neat. Inside the attention scores, every "not allowed" future link is set to $-\infty$ (minus infinity) before the softmax. Since $e^{-\infty}=0$, softmax gives those positions exactly zero weight. (That is the optional "Mask" box back in Figure 2.)

7.5  Embeddings, weight tying, and the final softmax

Two last details, from the top and bottom of the diagram.

Shared embedding weights. The model uses learned embeddings (§3.1) to turn tokens into vectors at the input. At the output, it needs to turn vectors back into word chances. The paper ties these together: the input embedding grid, the output embedding grid, and the final layer before softmax all share the same numbers. This saves memory and tends to help quality. The embeddings are also multiplied by $\sqrt{d_{model}}$ so their size matches the positional encodings (next section).

The output step. At the very top, the decoder's final vectors pass through a Linear layer (which maps them to the size of the vocabulary, about 37,000) and then a Softmax. This gives a chance for every possible next word. The model picks a word from these chances, adds it to the output, and runs again — the auto-regressive loop from §3.4.

Section 8

Positional encoding — putting order back in

The parallel design creates a subtle problem. Attention treats its inputs as a set with no order. If you shuffled the words, the attention math would give the same blend, because it just compares every word to every word. But word order carries meaning (§2)! An RNN got order for free by reading in order. The Transformer gave that up to gain speed. So we have to put order back in by hand.

The fix is positional encoding. Before the first layer, we add a special vector to each word's embedding. This vector encodes where the word sits in the sentence. It is the same length as the embedding (512), so they just add together. Now "cat" at position 2 and "cat" at position 9 enter the network as different vectors, and attention can use position as a clue.

The paper builds these position vectors from sine and cosine waves of different speeds — one speed per number in the vector:

$$PE_{(pos,\,2i)}=\sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{\,2i/d_{model}}}\right)\qquad PE_{(pos,\,2i+1)}=\cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{\,2i/d_{model}}}\right)$$

Don't let it scare you. Here $pos$ is the position (0, 1, 2, …) and $i$ picks which number in the vector. Each number is a wave. Low numbers wave fast; high numbers wave slowly. A word's full position vector is a snapshot of all these waves at its spot — a unique "fingerprint" for that slot.

Intuition · why waves?

The authors picked waves for a handy reason. The position $pos{+}k$ can always be written as a simple fixed mix of position $pos$. That makes it easy for the model to learn relative offsets ("the word three slots back"), which often matters more than the exact position. They also hoped — and it mostly held true — that smooth waves would help the model handle sentences longer than any it saw in training. They also tried learned position vectors and got almost the same results (see the test in §11), so the choice is partly about elegance.

Section 9

Why self-attention? The trade-off table

Section 4 of the paper defends the design by comparing self-attention against recurrent and convolutional layers on three things: how much work each layer does, how much can be done at the same time (fewer ordered steps is better), and how far a signal must travel to link two faraway words (shorter is easier to learn — remember §3.5).

Table 1 — Cost and reach of different layer types. n = number of words, d = size of each vector, k = convolution window size, r = size of the local neighbourhood for restricted attention.
Layer typeWork per layerOrdered stepsLongest path between two words
Self-attentionO(n²·d)O(1) — fixedO(1) — fixed
Recurrent (RNN)O(n·d²)O(n) — grows with lengthO(n) — grows with length
ConvolutionalO(k·n·d²)O(1)O(logk n)
Self-attention (restricted)O(r·n·d)O(1)O(n/r)

The two columns that win the argument are the last two. Self-attention needs only a fixed, small number of ordered steps (everything else happens in parallel — unlike the RNN's $n$ steps). And the path between any two words is just length 1 (a word reaches any other word directly, instead of $n$ hops in an RNN). These are exactly the two RNN weaknesses from §3.5, both fixed.

The honest cost

There is a catch worth knowing, because it drives a lot of today's research. Self-attention's work grows with $n^2$ (n times n), where $n$ is the number of words. That is because every word attends to every word. For sentence-length inputs, that is still cheaper than an RNN. But for very long inputs (whole books, or large images), the $n^2$ part becomes the slow bottleneck. The authors already hint at a fix — "restricted" attention that only looks at nearby words (the last row of the table). Ten years of work on faster, longer attention grew out of exactly this worry.

One more benefit the authors point out: you can see inside the model. Because attention gives clear weights, you can literally look at what each head pays attention to. That is what the pictures in the next section show.

Section 10

How it was trained

The training recipe matters, because these exact choices became the template others copied. None of it is strange. It is a set of sensible choices that are now standard.

Data & batching

It was trained on standard translation datasets: English–German (about 4.5 million sentence pairs, with a shared set of about 37,000 word-pieces) and the bigger English–French (about 36 million pairs, 32,000 pieces). Sentence pairs of similar length were grouped together to save time, with about 25,000 word-pieces in each batch.

Hardware & schedule

One machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. The base model trained in about 12 hours (100,000 steps). The big model took about 3.5 days (300,000 steps). Compared with the systems it beat, this was very cheap — a key point of the paper.

Optimiser & the warm-up learning rate

They used the Adam optimiser (a standard, smart way to turn the training knobs from §3.2). It came with an unusual learning-rate plan. (The learning rate sets how big each training step is.) First, raise the learning rate slowly for the first 4,000 "warm-up" steps. Then lower it bit by bit, in proportion to $1/\sqrt{\text{step}}$.

$$lrate = d_{model}^{-0.5}\cdot \min\!\left(\text{step}^{-0.5},\ \text{step}\cdot \text{warmup}^{-1.5}\right)$$ paper eq. (3)

Regularisation (stopping memorisation)

  • Dropout (rate 0.1): during training, randomly set some numbers to zero. This forces the model not to lean too hard on any single path. It is used on each part's output and on the embedding-plus-position sums.
  • Label smoothing (0.1): instead of teaching the model to be 100% sure of the correct word, aim for about 90% sure. This slightly hurts one score (the model is on purpose less over-confident) but improves real translation quality.
From zero · overfitting

A model "overfits" when it memorises the quirks of its training data instead of learning the general pattern. It is like a student who memorises old exams but cannot answer new questions. Dropout and label smoothing are two cheap forms of insurance against that.

Section 11

Results and the evidence

There are three claims to back up: it is better, it is cheaper, and it works on more than one task. The paper delivers on all three.

1 · Translation quality (and cost)

Quality is measured in BLEU. This is a score from 0 to 100 for how well a machine translation matches translations done by people. Higher is better, and even a single point is a real difference.

Table 2 (selected) — BLEU on the 2014 test sets, plus training cost in number of operations. The Transformer leads on quality at a fraction of the cost.
ModelEN–DE BLEUEN–FR BLEUTraining cost (operations)
GNMT + RL (Google, RNN)24.639.921.4·10²⁰
ConvS2S (convolutional)25.1640.461.5·10²⁰
Previous best (group of models)26.3641.291.2·10²¹
Transformer (base)27.338.13.3·10¹⁸
Transformer (big)28.441.82.3·10¹⁹

The big Transformer set a new record on English–German (28.4 BLEU, beating even groups of models by more than 2 points) and on English–French (41.8). And it used about 10 to 100 times less training work than the models it beat. Even the small base model beat earlier published systems. Better and cheaper at the same time is rare, and that is what made everyone pay attention.

2 · What actually mattered (the tests)

The authors changed one ingredient at a time (their Table 3) to see what really carried the weight:

  • Number of heads: a single head was about 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting — so multi-head helps. But too many heads (32) also hurt. About 8 was the sweet spot.
  • Key size $d_k$: making it smaller hurt quality. This suggests that judging how well a query and key match is genuinely hard, and it needs room.
  • Model size: bigger was reliably better. (This was an early hint of the whole "scaling" era to come.)
  • Dropout: removing it hurt a lot — overfitting is real.
  • Positional encoding: learned position vectors did about the same as the waves (§8). So the choice was safe either way.

3 · It works on more than one task

To show the Transformer is not just a translation trick, they used it on a very different language task: parsing. Parsing means working out the grammar structure of a sentence as a tree. With little task-specific tuning, it did as well as or better than strong specialised models, even with limited training data (their Table 4). The design is general.

Seeing attention work

Because attention shows its weights (§9), the appendix draws pictures of them — and this is the most satisfying payoff in the paper.

In the full appendix, other heads are shown sorting out pronouns (an "its" clearly pointing to its noun) and following sentence structure. This is concrete proof for the §5 claim that different heads focus on different relationships.

Section 12

The legacy: what this paper unleashed

The paper modestly ends by saying the authors are "excited about the future of attention-based models" and plan to try them on images, audio, and video. That undersells what happened. The Transformer became the foundation of modern AI:

  • GPT (2018 onward) took the decoder half and scaled it up into the language models behind ChatGPT and Claude. The auto-regressive, masked, next-word loop you learned in §3.4 and §7.4 is how these models write.
  • BERT (2018) took the encoder half for deep language understanding, and changed search and language tools.
  • Vision, audio, protein folding (AlphaFold), code, robotics — the same design, used on "tokens" that are not words, now covers almost every kind of data, just as the paper hoped.
  • The scaling era. The finding that "bigger is better," plus the Transformer's GPU-friendly parallel design (§3.5, §9), made it the natural choice for training ever-larger models — the main project of every frontier lab today.
Why this is the right paper to start with

Almost everything a frontier lab works on grows out of a choice made in these eight pages: handling longer context (the $O(n^2)$ problem of §9), stable training (the residuals and warm-up of §7.2 and §10), faster output, scaling laws, and seeing inside models (reading attention, §11). Understand this paper well, and the rest of the field has a backbone to hang on.

Section 13

Glossary — the words, in one place

Token
The smallest piece of text a model works with — a word or a word-piece.
Embedding
The learned list of numbers that stands for a token; here, 512 numbers.
Vector
A list of numbers; you can picture it as a point or an arrow in space.
Dot product
Multiply the matching numbers of two vectors and add them up; it measures how alike they are.
Weight matrix
A grid of learned numbers that defines a layer (a step that stretches and shifts the input).
ReLU
The simple bend max(0, x): keep positive numbers, turn negative numbers into zero.
Softmax
Turns a list of scores into positive weights that add up to 1.
Query / Key / Value (Q/K/V)
For each word: what it is looking for / its matchable label / the content it offers. The three vectors attention runs on.
Attention
For each query, a weighted blend of all values, with more weight on the keys that match the query.
Self-attention
Attention where Q, K, and V all come from the same sentence (it looks at itself).
Multi-head attention
Several attention steps run side by side with their own weights, then combined; here 8 heads.
Encoder / Decoder
The half that reads and understands the input / the half that writes the output one word at a time.
Auto-regressive
Writing each new word using the words already written.
Causal mask
Stops the decoder from looking at future words (sets those scores to minus infinity).
Residual connection
Adding a part's input to its output, to make deep stacks easier to train.
Layer normalisation
Re-centring and re-scaling a layer's output to keep the numbers steady.
Feed-forward network (FFN)
Two linear layers plus ReLU, used on each word on its own (512 → 2048 → 512).
Positional encoding
Position-based vectors (waves) added to embeddings so word order is kept.
BLEU
A score from 0 to 100 for translation quality; higher is better.
dmodel, dk, dv, dff, h, N
The model's main sizes — see the panel below.

Section 14

Study checklist — can you explain each of these?

You have understood the paper when you can answer these without notes. Treat them as self-test questions.

  • Why did RNNs hit a wall, and which two problems does the Transformer fix?
  • What are queries, keys, and values — and where do they come from?
  • Walk through the four steps of scaled dot-product attention from memory.
  • Why divide by √dk? What goes wrong if you don't?
  • Why use several heads, and why does using 8 cost about the same as using 1?
  • Name the three places attention is used, and how Q/K/V differ in each.
  • What do "Add & Norm" and the feed-forward network each add to a layer?
  • How does the causal mask work, and why does the decoder need it?
  • Why is positional encoding needed at all, and why waves?
  • What does the $n^2$ cost in Table 1 mean, and why does it drive modern research?
  • In one sentence: why is this the design behind today's AI models?
Going deeper

Good next reads after this paper: The Illustrated Transformer (Jay Alammar) for more pictures, The Annotated Transformer (Harvard NLP) to see it built line by line in code, then the GPT and BERT papers to see the two halves taken in different directions. If you want to build one yourself, Andrej Karpathy's "Let's build GPT" video makes this design from scratch.

"Attention Is All You Need" — Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser, Polosukhin (2017)
